Mapping detector systems typically use a spatial contextual sensor such as GPS to associate radiation levels with the measured position, and by moving the detector system, radiation levels can be associated with positions on the map (often referred to as creating ‘breadcrumbs’), or these levels can be interpolated to create a map. The implementation of radiation mapping by Remote Sensing Laboratories (RSL) onboard aerial assets within the Aerial Monitoring System (AMS) program is an excellent example [11]. The algorithms run by the AMS also typically correct for the height of the detector system above ground-level by using a radar altimeter to measure height and implementing an exponential function to relate a measured gamma rate to a ground-level equivalent [11]. An aspect of SDF is the timeliness with which algorithms can complete analysis of collected data, we refer to the time between data collection and algorithm completion as ‘lag’. For the purposes of this report, we define a few terms related to timeliness and lag: • Real-time: So fast, if it were faster nothing would be different. • Near real-time: Happening during measurement and lag is small (typically order 1s). • Online: Happening during measurement (may be real-time, near real-time, or have some appreciable lag). • Offline: Algorithms that are designed to be run once on the entirety of a collected dataset, rather than online. Run-times may be seconds, minutes, hours or days. • Accumulating versus fixed lag: some algorithms are able to “keep up”, but take a certain amount of time to run. Such algorithms have fixed lag. Other algorithms accumulate lag as more data is processed. The SDF algorithms were initially implemented to run in near real-time. The initial SLAM algorithms would have about 1s of fixed lag and could be configured to not accumulate additional lag, at the expense of reliability. SLAM algorithms achieve this low and fixed lag by creating sub- maps which grow independently and are reconciled through ‘loop-closure’. Infrequent (or no) loop LBNL Report #2001653 closure mitigates accumulating lag, but as runs become longer infrequent loop-closure can result in SLAM maps that are clearly erroneous owing to accumulating sensor error. Due to reasons explained in Sec. 2.2, the SDF processing algorithms that leverage the SLAM solutions to create on-line data products would typically have accumulating lags that started at less than a second, but could increase with both geometric size and the number of radiation counts that were being processed. Thesealgorithmswouldeventuallybecomenotusefulforproducingonlinedataproducts due to the accumulated lag. As a result, the earliest SDF prototypes were typically operated for runs of ≲15min duration, in order to maintain online data product generation.
